title: Comic Fantasy Needs Rules Too
body:
The temptation in comic fantasy is to let magic do anything the joke requires. It kills the mystery plot stone dead — if magic is unlimited, the culprit could be anyone and the evidence means nothing. Give Brian a Hand runs on magic that is petty, bureaucratic and unreliable, which is exactly what a whodunnit needs.

Constraint is also where the comedy lives. A spell that only works on Thursdays is funnier than one that always works.

title: The Reluctant Hero Is Not a Lazy Hero
body:
Brian does not want to solve anything. That is the joke and also the problem: a protagonist who refuses to act stalls the story. The fix is to make refusal cost him more than participation — every time he tries to go home, the case follows him there.

Reluctance then becomes a source of momentum rather than a brake on it, and the reader roots for someone who is, at heart, just tired.

title: Writing a Mystery Readers Can Actually Solve
body:
Fair play is the contract. Every clue is on the page before the reveal, even in a world with talking furniture. The comedy is not permitted to hide the evidence — it can only distract from it, which is a different and more honest trick.

The test on revision: could a careful reader, ignoring the jokes, have named the culprit a chapter early? If yes, the mystery works and the humour is doing its proper job.
